definitions.definition: The principle (essence) of the Word: Bhartṛhari's name for Brahman, without beginning or end, which appears as things (VP 1.1).

literal: the word-principle / reality of the word

definitions.definition: Brahman as the Word: the Word-principle (śabdatattva) that appears as the world and permeates all cognition; its highest accessible level is paśyantī (VP 1.1, 1.123, 1.142).

The unmanifest sound arising from the dividing supreme bindu; not the word nor the meaning (both insentient) but the consciousness of all beings, which dwells in the body as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.11–14).

equivalents.note: duplicate id used by U19 for the same term; to be merged
the music treatises' nāda-brahman is described in the same words ('the consciousness of all beings') as the mantra manuals' śabda-brahman

definitions.definition: The meaning-bearing word itself, partless and without sequence, distinct from the sounds (dhvani/nāda) that manifest it; it 'bursts forth' as meaning in the intellect when the sounds have planted their seeds (VP 1.44; Mahābhāṣya on P 1.1.70). The later grammarians count eight kinds and hold the sentence-sphoṭa alone real.

literal: burst, that from which meaning bursts forth

equivalents.standpoint: Nāgeśa's placement of the levels of speech in the body
equivalents.note: Nāgeśa identifies the meaning-conveying sphoṭa with speech at the madhyamā level

definitions.definition: The audible sound that manifests the sphoṭa; Patañjali calls it a quality of the word (on P 1.1.70); the grammarians distinguish the primary sound that reveals the sphoṭa from the secondary sound responsible for differences of speed and length.

Suggestion: the implied meaning (pratīyamāna) conveyed beyond denotation, and poetry in which it predominates; named after the grammarians' dhvani that manifests the sphoṭa; threefold — suggested fact, figure and rasa (DhĀ 1.1, 1.4, 1.13).

equivalents.note: vyañjanā is the power, dhvani the suggested sense or the poetry

definitions.definition: The power of suggestion, a function of words beyond denotation (abhidhā) and indication (lakṣaṇā) by which the implied sense and rasa are conveyed; denied by Mahimabhaṭṭa (inference) and by Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas.
Accepted by Nāgeśa as a third power of words beside denotation and indication.
Denotation, the primary power of a word to convey its conventional meaning; the first of the three powers (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā).
The primary power (śakti) of words; for the grammarians grounded in the eternal relation of word and meaning.
Indication, the secondary power by which a word conveys a meaning connected with its primary sense when the primary sense does not fit ('a village on the Ganges').
Purport: Dhanika and others hold that rasa and implied senses are conveyed by the purport of the sentence, making a separate power of suggestion unnecessary.

The flash of intuition in which a sentence's unitary meaning is grasped, indescribable even by its possessor; also the instinct by which animals act (the cuckoo's song, nest-building); sixfold by source (VP 2.143–152).
Poetic genius: the cause of poetry (śakti, KP 1.3); for Rājaśekhara twofold, creative (kārayitrī) and appreciative (bhāvayitrī).

The highest of Bhartṛhari's three levels of speech: undivided, all sequence withdrawn, the inner light of its own form, subtle and imperishable (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); identified by the grammarians with the Word-Brahman.
The second of four levels of speech, above madhyamā and below parā; placed by Nāgeśa and the tantric manuals at the navel.

equivalents.note: the grammarians treat paśyantī as the supreme; Somānanda and Utpaladeva place parā vāk above it

definitions.definition: The middle level of speech: its material is the intellect alone; it follows sequence and goes beyond the working of breath (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the heart, the level at which the sphoṭa conveys meaning.
Articulated, audible speech, produced when breath strikes the places of articulation, whose letters are grasped by the hearer (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the throat and mouth.
Accepted by Nāgeśa as the fourth, highest level of speech, motionless and unmanifest in the root centre — a level not named by Bhartṛhari.
The supreme level of speech, identical with the Goddess (Śakti) as consciousness, above paśyantī.
Speech as the consciousness of beings, within and without, moving them to all activity; when it departs a being is like a log (VP 1, from memory).
The word-nature of awareness: eternal, it makes recognition (pratyavamarśa) possible; without it light would not illumine (VP 1.124).
Reflective recognition, the word-natured 'grasping back' that makes a cognition determinate; the function of speech in awareness (VP 1.124).

equivalents.note: the Pratyabhijñā's vimarśa (reflexive awareness as supreme speech) develops Bhartṛhari's pratyavamarśa

definitions.definition: Abstraction: the division of the sentence into words and of words into stems and affixes, a device of grammatical analysis with no ultimate reality, since the sentence is partless (VP 1.73; kāṇḍa 2).
The sentence, for the grammarians the primary indivisible unit of meaning (vākya-sphoṭa); Bhartṛhari lists eight rival definitions (VP 2.1–2).
The meaning of the sentence, grasped as a flash of pratibhā distinct from the word-meanings (VP 2.143).
The relation of word and meaning, eternal and not made by anyone (Kātyāyana's first vārttika; VP 1.23; 3.3 'fitness', yogyatā).

literal: the relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: Fitness: the natural capacity of a word to express its meaning, the eternal relation between them (VP 3.3).
The time-power of the Word-Brahman, its independent power (svātantrya) by which sequence and the six modifications of being appear (VP 1.3; 3.9).
The universal, which words denote; the true part of things; ultimately Being (sattā) itself (VP 3.1).

Substance: synonymous with self, thing, own nature, body and reality; ultimately the Real that all words denote, as gold is denoted by all ornament-words (VP 3.2); Vyāḍi held that words denote the individual substance.
Form, universal: Vājapyāyana held that words denote the ākṛti (Mahābhāṣya on P 1.2.64).
Being, the great universal (mahāsattā) that all words finally denote, identified with Brahman (VP 3.1).
The 'turning out' or unfolding by which the Word-principle appears as things (VP 1.1); whether this means an unreal appearance (as later Advaita) or a manifestation is debated.
Bhavabhūti: the one rasa, compassion, takes different forms (vivarta) as water takes the forms of eddies, bubbles and waves (UR 3.47).
The refinement or purification of words through grammar, which is 'the attainment of the supreme self' (VP 1, verse number uncertain).
'Yoga preceded by the word': the path in which correct usage of words and knowledge of their nature lead to union with the Word-Brahman (Vṛtti on VP 1).

A correct word (as taught by grammar), whose knowing use brings merit, as opposed to a corrupt form (apaśabda); 'a single word well known and well used is a wish-granting cow in heaven' (Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.84).
A corrupt or incorrect word-form (e.g. vernacular variants of 'gauḥ'); its use is forbidden in ritual contexts and the Asuras were defeated for mispronunciation (Mahābhāṣya Paspaśā).
Grammar as the nearest to Brahman, the highest austerity, the door to liberation and remedy for the impurities of speech (VP 1.11–16).
Scripture and unbroken tradition, without which dharma cannot be established by reasoning (VP 1.30).
Reasoning, unstable when unsupported by scripture: what is inferred by the skilled is refuted by the more skilled (VP 1.34).
The imperishable Word-Brahman (VP 1.1) and the syllable/letter.
The letter: for the grammarians not a real part of the word, which is partless (VP 1.73).
The letters as the manifestation of śabda-brahman through kuṇḍalinī (ŚT 1.14); gathered as the fifty mātṛkās.

Aesthetic relish: the stable emotion made relishable by the union of determinants, consequents and transient states, tasted by the sensitive spectator as food is tasted (NŚ 6 rasa-sūtra); eight in drama (NŚ 6.15), nine with śānta; 'twin of tasting Brahman' (SD 3.2).
The emotional flavour that notes, rāgas and dance are to evoke; the music treatises assign notes and rāgas to rasas.

Emotional state; so called because, with speech, body and sattva, it 'brings into being' (bhāvayati) the meaning of the poem (NŚ 7.1–3); of three kinds — eight stable, thirty-three transient, eight involuntary; love directed to gods, gurus and kings remains a bhāva (KP 4).

literal: state, feeling; 'that which brings into being'
notes: Disambiguated from trm:bhava (used by other units for Sāṃkhya's bhāvas, Rudra's name 'Bhava' and the Gauḍīya stage 'bhāva').

definitions.definition: Determinant: the cause of an emotion in drama or poetry — its object and support (ālambana) and its excitants (uddīpana) (NŚ 6–7).

literal: that which causes to be felt
notes: Disambiguated from trm:vibhava (Pāñcarātra 'vibhava', the Lord's descents); U16's aesthetic use of trm:vibhava belongs here.

definitions.definition: Consequent: the outward signs by which an emotion is known — glances, gestures, movements (NŚ 6–7).

notes: Disambiguated from trm:anubhava ('experience'); U16's aesthetic use of trm:anubhava belongs here.

definitions.definition: The thirty-three transient states that move within the stable emotion, from despondency (nirveda) to deliberation (NŚ 6.18–21).
The stable emotion that becomes rasa: love, laughter, grief, anger, energy, fear, disgust, wonder (NŚ 6.17), and for śānta calm, dispassion or knowledge of reality.
The eight involuntary states arising from sattva (concentrated mind): paralysis, sweat, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting (NŚ 6.22).

The rasa of peace, leading to liberation, whose stable emotion is calm (śama, NŚ śānta passage; SD 3.245), dispassion (nirveda, KP 4) or knowledge of reality — the self itself (Abhinavagupta); denied as a dramatic rasa by Dhanañjaya.

equivalents.note: poetics praises the relish of śānta; Gauḍapāda (MK 3.45) calls tasting the bliss of samādhi (rasāsvāda) an obstacle to be given up — the same word, opposite valuations

definitions.definition: 'One with heart': the sensitive, cultivated spectator or reader whose mind, polished by repeated study of poetry, can become one with the work and relish rasa (NŚ 6.32–33; DhĀ 1.1).

Generalization: the process by which determinants and emotions shown in the art-work are freed from belonging to a particular person, time and place, so that the spectator relishes them impersonally (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka; Abhinavagupta).
'Chewing': the relishing through which rasa exists — for Abhinavagupta rasa is not a thing produced but consists in this relishing and lasts as long as it lasts.
Wonder, the life of rasa (SD 3.3); for Abhinavagupta the self-relishing of consciousness in aesthetic experience; for Viśvanātha's ancestor Nārāyaṇa the reason why the marvellous is the one rasa.
Repose: drama gives rest to the afflicted (NŚ 1.114); in Abhinavagupta's aesthetics rasa is consciousness at rest in itself.

'Twin brother of tasting Brahman': Viśvanātha's description of rasa (SD 3.2), following Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's comparison of aesthetic enjoyment with the tasting of the supreme Brahman — akin to it, not identical with it.
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's power of poetic language to 'make present' its content in generalized form (reported by Abhinavagupta).
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's power of poetic language to make the rasa enjoyed in a state pervaded by sattva, akin to tasting Brahman (reported by Abhinavagupta).

The seven obstacles to aesthetic relish listed by Abhinavagupta (lack of credibility, particularity of time and place, absorption in one's own feelings, lack of means, lack of clarity, non-predominance, doubt).
Calm, the stable emotion of śānta in the Nāṭyaśāstra's śānta passage and in the Sāhityadarpaṇa (3.245).
Despondency, world-weariness: the first of the thirty-three transient states (NŚ 6.18), made by Mammaṭa the stable emotion of śānta.
Knowledge of reality, which Abhinavagupta makes the stable emotion of śānta: it is the self itself (Abhinavabhāratī).
Self-regard, 'I-ness': for Bhoja the one true rasa, called śṛṅgāra, of which the named rasas are developments.
Poetry: word and meaning together (Bhāmaha 1.16); faultless word and meaning with qualities (KP 1.4); a sentence whose soul is rasa (SD 1.3); a word conveying a charming meaning (Jagannātha).
Figure of speech ('ornament') of sound or sense; for Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin the essence of poetic beauty, for Ānandavardhana subordinate to rasa.
Style, a special arrangement of words (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī); for Vāmana the soul of poetry (KAS 1.2.6).
The qualities of poetry — sweetness (mādhurya), vigour (ojas) and clarity (prasāda) in the later scheme, ten in Daṇḍin and Vāmana — which for Mammaṭa belong to rasa as heroism belongs to the self.
Faults of word, sense and rasa that diminish poetry (SD 1.3); treated at length in KP 7.
Oblique, striking expression; for Bhāmaha the basis of all figures, for Kuntaka the life of poetry.
Propriety, appropriateness of every element to rasa and context; for Kṣemendra the life of poetry.
Drama, the 'fifth Veda' made by Brahmā for all classes, the representation of the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.12, 1.107).
Acting, 'carrying towards' the spectators: fourfold — bodily (āṅgika), verbal (vācika), costume and make-up (āhārya) and involuntary states (sāttvika) (NŚ 6.23).
Pure dance, movement without representational meaning; with song and instrument part of saṅgīta (ŚR 1.1.21).
Expressive dance that conveys bhāva through gesture and glance.
The preliminaries of a performance — songs, instrumental pieces and the benediction (nāndī) — offered to please the gods (NŚ 5).
Song, instrumental music and dance taken together (ŚR 1.1.21).

The two kinds of music: mārga, the 'sought-out' divine music fixed by Brahmā and Bharata that gives well-being when performed before Śiva, and deśī, regional music that delights people (ŚR 1.1.22–23; Bṛhaddeśī 13).
The sacred music of the gods (dear to the gods, NŚ 28), of notes, rhythm and words; the upaveda of the Sāmaveda.

Sound, on which song, instrument, dance, speech and the world depend (ŚR 1.2.1–2; Bṛhaddeśī 16–17); born of the union of breath (na) and fire (da) (ŚR 1.3.6); twofold, struck and unstruck, and fivefold by its places in the body.
The sounds that manifest the sphoṭa and plant their seeds in the intellect (VP 1).
The second emanation after Śakti (ŚT 1.7), and in the threefold bindu the union of Śiva and Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9).

Brahman as sound: the consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world, bliss without a second, worshipped through nāda (ŚR 1.3.1–2); Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the supreme Śakti and Śiva are its forms (Bṛhaddeśī 17–18).
Worship of nāda: through it Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara are worshipped (ŚR 1.3.2); the unstruck nāda by sages on the guru's path, the struck nāda through music (ŚR 1.2.165–167).
Struck sound, produced by contact (voice, instrument); in music the means that delights people and breaks worldly bondage (ŚR 1.2.3, 1.2.167).
Unstruck sound, worshipped by sages by the path taught by the guru — an easy means to liberation, but without charm (rakti) for ordinary people (ŚR 1.2.165–166).
The body as the place where nāda becomes manifest; hence the Saṅgītaratnākara's section on 'the origin of the body' (piṇḍotpatti) (ŚR 1.2.3).
Charm, the quality of colouring the mind with delight, lacking in the unstruck nāda and present in music (ŚR 1.2.166); cognate with rāga.
One of the twenty-two audible pitch-divisions of the octave, produced in twenty-two channels at the heart (ŚR 1.3.8–9); the basis from which the svaras arise.

A note: that which arises right after the śruti, smooth and resonant, and of itself delights the listener (ŚR 1.3.24–25); seven — ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, niṣāda (sa ri ga ma pa dha ni).
A 'village' or system of seven notes with fixed śruti-intervals — ṣaḍja-grāma and madhyama-grāma (and a lost gāndhāra-grāma) — the basis of the mūrchanās and jātis.
A sequence of the seven notes of a grāma beginning from each note in turn, basis of the ancient modes.
One of the eighteen ancient melodic types of gāndharva music, precursors of the rāgas.
A melodic entity: that particular sound adorned with notes and melodic movement which colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281).
Rhythm and metrical cycle measured by claps and beats; the subject of the fifth chapter of the Saṅgītaratnākara.
Tempo: the rest between the actions of tāla, slow, middle and fast.

notes: Musical sense; the term also means 'absorption' in yoga (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: The stringed instrument of Sarasvatī and Nārada; demonstration device for the śrutis (ŚR 1.3.11–22); one who knows its playing goes the way of liberation (YājS 3.115).
Ornamental oscillation or inflection of a note, essential to the rendering of a rāga.
A parent scale under which rāgas are grouped; Veṅkaṭamakhin's scheme of seventy-two melas.
Devotional song, especially singing the Lord's names and deeds, alone or in a group; in Karṇāṭaka music also the name of a composed song form (kṛti).
Devotional singing, typically congregational, of songs and names of the deity, from 'bhaj' (to share in, worship).

equivalents.note: duplicate id (Hindi form) used by U27; to be merged

definitions.definition: A sacred formula made of the letters (mātṛkā), each with its seer, metre, deity, seed, power and pin; mantras proper have male deities, vidyās female; they are male, female or neuter by their endings (ŚT 2.57–59) and fiery or lunar (ŚT 2.60–63).

literal: instrument of thought (traditional etymology: that which protects (trā) the one who reflects (man))

definitions.definition: A mantra whose deity is female (ŚT 2.58); e.g. the Śrīvidyā.

Seed-syllable: a monosyllabic mantra (often ending in the nasal bindu) that contains a deity or element in seed form — e.g. laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ for the elements, hrīṃ, śrīṃ, klīṃ, aiṃ for goddesses; in the threefold bindu, bīja is Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9).
The 'pin' or 'bolt' of a mantra, named with its seed (bīja) and power (śakti) in the preliminary formula before recitation.
The declaration before recitation of a mantra's seer (ṛṣi), metre (chandas), deity (devatā), seed, power and pin and the purpose for which it is applied.

The 'little mothers': the fifty (or fifty-one) letters from a to kṣa, manifestations of śabda-brahman through kuṇḍalinī (ŚT 1.14), the body of the Goddess and of every mantra; placed on the body in mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Placing: the installation of letters, mantras and deities on parts of the body by touch and visualization (mātṛkā-nyāsa, ṛṣyādi-nyāsa, the six-limbed nyāsa), making the body divine before worship and japa.
Repetition of a mantra: loud (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu) or mental (mānasa), each superior to the previous (Vāyavīya Saṃhitā quoted in the Padārthādarśa).
Audible repetition with correct tones and clear syllables; ten times better than ritual sacrifice.
Whispered repetition, lips moving slightly, barely audible; a hundred times better.
Mental repetition of the series of letters with remembrance of meaning, without movement of head, tongue or lips; a thousand times better.

The preliminary 'going before': a course of a fixed number of repetitions of a mantra (commonly counted by its syllables), with fire offering, libations, sprinkling and feeding brāhmaṇas in fixed proportions, by which the mantra is mastered before use.
A defect of a mantra (cut, obstructed, powerless, asleep and forty-five more, ŚT 2.64–70) that makes it fail to protect the practitioner.
The ten purifications of a mantra — generation, enlivening, striking, awakening, consecration, cleansing, strengthening, satiation, kindling, guarding (ŚT 2.112–113).
Guarding: the non-disclosure of the mantra being repeated, itself the tenth purification (ŚT 2.122).
Success or perfection in a mantra, when after purification and puraścaraṇa the mantra 'awakens' and gives its fruit — enjoyment and liberation.
The 'consciousness' or life of a mantra: without it a mantra is only letters; it is awakened by the guru's transmission, purification and the practitioner's absorption.
Initiation in which a qualified guru gives the mantra to a qualified, tested disciple (ŚT 2.141–153).
Śabda-brahman in the body: consciousness dwelling coiled in the middle of the body, from which the letters arise (ŚT 1.14).
The power of Brahman in the root centre which, straightened up to the brahmarandhra, bestows nectar (ŚR 1.2.121–122).
The 'point' arising from nāda (ŚT 1.7), which divides into bindu, nāda and bīja — Śiva, their union and Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9); in mantras the nasal dot (anusvāra).

Oṃ, the 'tāra', prefixed to mantras; its letters a, u, m are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, and its subtle phases (bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, unmanā) are traversed in meditative utterance.
The one word from which the Veda's knowledge springs, opposed to no doctrine (VP 1.9, low confidence).

equivalents.note: same syllable; duplicate ids to be merged
same syllable; duplicate ids to be merged

definitions.definition: The Sāvitrī mantra (RV 3.62.10) with Oṃ and the vyāhṛtis, repeated at the twilights, and the Goddess Gāyatrī who is its deity; the mantra manuals give its seer (Viśvāmitra), metre (gāyatrī) and deity (Savitṛ), its nyāsa and puraścaraṇa.
The 'three-eyed' Śiva of the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya verse (RV 7.59.12), whose mantra, with added seed-syllables, is repeated for protection from death and disease.
The final, 'beyond-mind' phase in the subtle utterance of Oṃ, where sound dissolves into the supreme.
The rosary for counting japa; also the 'garland of letters' a to kṣa (akṣa-mālā) with which mental japa is counted.
The supreme Lord, splendid with being, consciousness and bliss, with parts (sakala), source of Śakti, nāda and bindu (ŚT 1.7).
